passage: The school library was nearly empty at four o'clock, and the librarian kept glancing over her glasses. Shalini turned a page of her chemistry book without reading it. Across the table, Kavitha fidgeted with a pencil. "I only told Ritu. She promised she'd keep it." "It's not even the telling," Shalini said, her voice low. "I thought you were someone who would never do that. I'd have bet everything on it." Kavitha opened her mouth and closed it again. Shalini packed her bag and walked home slowly past the fruit sellers, feeling as if someone had moved away without leaving an address. By the gate she had decided she would still be Kavitha's classmate, but not the keeper of everything. And she would watch, more slowly this time, who earned a closer seat.

qa.q: Where do Shalini and Kavitha have their conversation?
qa.a: They talk at a table in the school library at four o'clock.

qa.q: What is Shalini feeling about Kavitha, and what hurts her more than the leak?
qa.a: Losing her picture of Kavitha as someone who would never do that. She says she would have bet everything on it, and she walks home feeling as if someone had moved away.

qa.q: What is a wise way for Shalini to go on from here?
qa.a: She can mourn the old picture, accept that Kavitha is flawed like anyone, and choose closer friends carefully instead of deciding that nobody can be trusted.

qa.q: How might Kavitha see the moment?
qa.a: Probably sorry and a little defensive. Saying she only told Ritu, and then falling silent, suggests she does not fully see that the loss matters more to Shalini than the secret.

grounding: Shalini grieves her image of a perfectly loyal friend more than the leak itself and chooses to trust more carefully rather than not at all.

passage: Sit, beta, and I'll tell you why I never followed the crowd. When I was fifteen, I'm Kiran in this story, I wanted Salma's table more than I wanted lunch. So I changed. I laughed at jokes I didn't find funny. I stopped bringing my sketchbook. I even copied the way they said "literally" every second word. For one month it felt like sunshine. Then Salma's group fell out over something small, and in the middle of it nobody could remember what I liked, because I had left nothing to remember. I sat alone with my tray, and the person I'd hidden was the only one I missed. A few weeks later I wandered into the art room, and a boy there said, "Oh, you're the one who draws bicycles!" I still have that sketchbook.

qa.q: What did Kiran stop bringing to school while trying to fit in with Salma's group?
qa.a: He stopped bringing his sketchbook.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when he sat alone with his tray?
qa.a: He felt the loss of himself. The person he had hidden was the only one he missed, and nobody in the group knew what he liked.

qa.q: What did Kiran learn about belonging that he could pass on?
qa.a: Belonging bought by erasing yourself is fragile, so it is worth looking for people who like the real you, as Kiran found in the art room.

qa.q: How might Salma's group have seen Kiran during that month?
qa.a: They probably saw someone easy to agree with but hard to know, since he had left nothing about himself for them to remember.

grounding: Kiran badly wanted the popular table and reshaped himself for it, then found that belonging built on self-erasure did not hold.

passage: The hostel dining hall smelled of dal and steam. Baljeet carried his tray toward the corner table where Kiran and the others sat. The talk stopped. Someone coughed. As soon as he sat on the end of the bench, a girl whispered something and the whole group burst out laughing, glancing at him and then away. Kiran stared at the tray, gripping the edge. Baljeet's face went hot, and for a second he wanted to laugh along just to belong. Instead he said, "I'll see you around," picked up his tray and walked to the chess club table by the window, where a junior moved a chair for him. That night he called his father from the warden's phone and told him everything, including the part that stung most.

qa.q: Where did Baljeet go after leaving the corner table?
qa.a: He walked to the chess club table by the window.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling as the group laughed?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed. His face went hot, and for a second he wanted to laugh along just to belong.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do that was wise?
qa.a: He left with dignity, found another table where he was welcome, and told his father what had happened.

qa.q: How does Kiran seem to experience that moment?
qa.a: Kiran stares at the tray and grips its edge, which may hint at discomfort or insecurity, though the passage does not say for sure.

grounding: Baljeet meets silence and inside-joke laughter from a clique, leaves with dignity, finds another group and tells someone he trusts.

passage: In the corridor of his school in Valparaiso, Rafael leaned on the lockers and said to his friend Tomas, "Look at them, all posing for the same photo. Completely empty." Tomas grinned. Rafael had said versions of it every week since Javier's group dropped him from their table last year. Then Javier came out of the sports hall, telling a joke to his friends. Nobody laughed. His smile stayed on for a second too long and then slid off, and he stared at the floor as he walked. Rafael stopped mid-sentence. His own sneer suddenly felt like a jacket he wore in the rain. "Do another one," Tomas said. "Nah," Rafael said. Next day he nodded to Javier at the water fountain, and Javier nodded back, surprised.

qa.q: Where was Rafael when he made the remark about the group posing for a photo?
qa.a: He was in the corridor of his school in Valparaiso, leaning on the lockers.

qa.q: What did Rafael realise when he saw Javier's smile slide off?
qa.a: He felt his own sneer was a kind of armour, like a jacket worn in the rain, and that Javier might be hurting too.

qa.q: What did Rafael choose to do instead of carrying on with the mockery?
qa.a: He stopped, refused Tomas's request for another one, and nodded to Javier the next day rather than adding bitter talk.

qa.q: How might Javier have felt when Rafael nodded at the fountain?
qa.a: Surprised and perhaps a little relieved, since he nodded back. After a joke that fell flat, a friendly nod may have meant a lot.

grounding: Rafael sneers at the popular group to protect himself, then sees the hurt behind the armour and refuses to become another exclusion machine.

passage: Class 9 observation note. Lalremsiami has seemed on edge for three weeks. She told me, "One day Damini saves me a seat and calls me her favourite. The next day she doesn't look at me, and I don't know what I did." On Tuesday Damini asked her to remove a group photo of another girl as "proof" she was on the group's side. Lalremsiami said she felt sick about it and did not do it. I asked her what she noticed about the pattern; she said the kindness always comes back after she gives in. I did not tell her what to feel about Damini. I suggested she keep sitting with the reading club girls, who are steady, and I have arranged a time for her with the counsellor. She left looking tired but lighter.

qa.q: What did Damini ask Lalremsiami to do on Tuesday?
qa.a: She asked her to remove a group photo of another girl as proof she was on the group's side.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling about the request?
qa.a: She felt sick about it. Her worry shows in how she says she does not know what she did when the warmth is withdrawn.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do that showed she had noticed the pattern?
qa.a: She refused the loyalty test and said the kindness always comes back after she gives in. The teacher then pointed her toward steadier friends and the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Damini see her own behaviour?
qa.a: Perhaps she wants to feel sure of her place in the group, and the passage does not say. To Lalremsiami, though, the warmth and coldness feel like a test.

grounding: A teacher's note records a clique leader granting and withdrawing warmth to keep Lalremsiami anxious, and her refusal and steadier friendships.

passage: Honestly, the best part was the walk down the corridor. People slowed down to see where I'd sit. I'm Irfan, I was fifteen, and I ran the back table. If a new kid came near, I'd say, "Seat's taken," and watch who noticed. It felt like holding a remote control. But at night I checked my phone for messages, sure that one wrong joke would make them all turn on me. That's what I was really doing, guarding a seat I was scared to lose. One Thursday Pooja came in alone with her lunch box. Everyone looked at me. My throat went dry. I moved my bag and said, "Pooja, here." Nobody said a word. Then Karan asked her about her lunch. Funny thing, the table didn't fall apart. It got bigger.

qa.q: What did Irfan say to a new kid who came near the back table?
qa.a: He said, "Seat's taken," and watched who noticed.

qa.q: What was Irfan really feeling underneath the power?
qa.a: Fear. He checked his phone at night, sure that one wrong joke would make them all turn on him, and he was guarding a seat he was scared to lose.

qa.q: How did Irfan use his influence in a better way?
qa.a: He moved his bag and invited Pooja to sit, which made room instead of shutting someone out.

qa.q: How might Pooja have seen Irfan's "Pooja, here"?
qa.a: She probably felt relief and surprise, since she came in alone and everyone looked at Irfan before he spoke. 😊

grounding: Irfan enjoys deciding who is in and out while privately fearing his place, and later uses his influence to include someone.

passage: At lunch in the Pune school canteen, Ishita watched Pranav walk up to the group's table with his tray. Riya turned her shoulder. Nimisha slid her bag onto the empty chair without a word. When Pranav asked, "Can I sit?" nobody answered, as if he had said it to the wall. Ishita stared at her rice, her ears warm. She wanted to say something, but the words sat like stones. Pranav stood for another second, then took his tray to the window ledge. All afternoon her stomach felt heavy. Next day in chemistry, she asked him quietly, "Want to be lab partners? I haven't picked yet." Pranav looked surprised. "Okay." It was a very small thing, and she was still shaking a little when she wrote her name on the sheet.

qa.q: Where did Pranav take his tray after nobody answered him?
qa.a: He took it to the window ledge.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling while the group ignored Pranav?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and stuck. Her ears went warm and she wanted to speak, but the words sat like stones.

qa.q: What small step did Ishita take, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: She asked Pranav to be her lab partner. It was a quiet way to include him without needing to confront the whole group.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt when Ishita asked him?
qa.a: Surprised, and maybe relieved to be noticed. He said "Okay" after looking surprised, after being ignored the day before.

grounding: Ishita stays silent while her group freezes someone out, feels guilty, and quietly befriends the excluded boy the next day.

passage: For weeks I had been on the edge of the group, always the one who arrived just after the joke. Then on Monday Mehak waved me over. "We're going for golgappa after school, come with us." I said yes so fast it embarrassed me. All day my chest felt light, and I kept smiling at the wall. But somewhere behind the relief there was a small, careful voice: why now? Would they still want me next week? At the golgappa stall I laughed a lot, and I was glad, but I also texted Anjali, my old bench mate, to say I'd still meet her on Saturday as usual. I don't know how long this will last, and I'm not going to pretend I do. I'm Disha, and I think I can enjoy it without throwing everything else away.

qa.q: Where did Mehak invite Disha to go after school?
qa.a: Mehak invited her for golgappa after school.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Disha have after the invitation?
qa.a: Relief, because her chest felt light and she kept smiling, and also wariness, because a small careful voice asked why now and whether they would still want her next week.

qa.q: How did Disha keep her older friendship safe?
qa.a: She texted Anjali to say she would still meet her on Saturday as usual, so she enjoys the new group without dropping an old friend.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel about the text?
qa.a: Probably glad to be remembered, and reassured that the new group has not replaced her. 🤍

grounding: After weeks on the edge, Disha is invited into the group and feels relief mixed with wariness while keeping her older friend.

passage: Mehak had heard that Sonali, a senior, loved old film songs, so by Wednesday her playlist was full of them. In the lunch line she stood two places behind Sonali and memorised everything she said: the joke about the physics teacher, the way she pushed her hair back, her opinion on mangoes. Everything Sonali said felt like a small gift. It was wonderful, like walking around lit from inside. When the dance rehearsal clashed with the library hour Sonali used, Mehak told the choreographer she was ill. That evening her friend Simran said, "You've missed two practices, and you don't even like those songs." Mehak went quiet. Then she saw Sonali on the stairs, arguing with her phone charger and looking simply tired. She wasn't a film star. She was a person. Mehak went back to rehearsal on Friday.

qa.q: What did Mehak fill her playlist with because of Sonali?
qa.a: She filled it with old film songs, because she had heard Sonali loved them.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling as she memorised Sonali's every word?
qa.a: Thrilled and dazzled. Everything Sonali said felt like a small gift, and it was like walking around lit from inside.

qa.q: What helped Mehak get her own life going again?
qa.a: Simran pointed out the missed practices, and seeing Sonali tired with a phone charger showed her a normal person. So she went back to rehearsal on Friday.

qa.q: How might Simran see Mehak's behaviour?
qa.a: She is probably worried. She says Mehak has missed two practices for songs she does not even like, so she sees her changing herself for someone else.

grounding: Mehak sees her crush as flawless and hangs on her words, then remembers Sonali is ordinary and returns to her own activities.

passage: Gurpreet's thumb had opened Nirmala's profile before he even decided to. Same photos, one new story about a rainy bus stop. He looked at it for the ninth time that evening, and the algebra on his desk stayed untouched. His mind kept circling like a fan: what did the rain mean, why hadn't she liked his comment, who was in the picture. When he thought of cycling past her lane "just to see", something in him went cold, because that felt wrong. He shut the phone in the drawer and called his cousin Harsh instead. "It's like being hungry for something that never fills me," he said. Harsh laughed kindly and said, "Come to the badminton court. Bring your racket, leave the phone." Gurpreet smashed shuttles until his arm ached, and it felt good.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do with his phone when he thought of cycling past Nirmala's lane?
qa.a: He shut it in the drawer and called his cousin Harsh.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet feel when he keeps checking her profile, and how can you tell?
qa.a: A restless hunger. He says it is like being hungry for something that never fills him, which shows he sees it as a loop that feeds itself.

qa.q: What steps helped Gurpreet in this passage?
qa.a: He put the phone away, talked to Harsh, and used his energy on the badminton court instead of checking or turning up at her lane.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see it if he had cycled past her lane uninvited?
qa.a: She would probably feel uneasy or watched, even if he meant no harm, so staying away respects her space.

grounding: Gurpreet checks his crush's profile constantly and cannot focus, and limits the checking, talks to a cousin and channels his energy elsewhere.
